title: Brock v. Roadway Express, Inc. (1987)
summary: Before ordering an employer to reinstate a discharged driver temporarily, the Secretary of Labor must tell the employer the substance of the evidence against it and let it respond, but need not hold an evidentiary hearing.
notes:
Key line: We conclude that minimum due process for the employer in this context requires notice of the employee's allegations, notice of the substance of the relevant supporting evidence, an opportunity to submit a written response, and an opportunity to meet with the investigator and present statements from rebuttal witnesses. (Justice Marshall, plurality)

Citation: 481 U.S. 252 (1987).

sections.Parties: The appellants were William Brock, Secretary of Labor, and other officials of the Department of Labor who administered the employee protection provision of the Surface Transportation Assistance Act of 1982. The appellee was Roadway Express, Inc., an interstate trucking company. The dispute arose from Roadway's discharge of one of its drivers, Jerry Hufstetler, who complained to the Department that he was fired for reporting safety violations. Andrew Pincus argued for the Secretary. Teamsters for a Democratic Union filed an amicus brief urging reversal of the judgment against the Secretary.
sections.Material Facts: Section 405 of the Surface Transportation Assistance Act forbids discharging a commercial motor carrier employee for refusing to operate a vehicle that does not meet safety standards or for filing safety complaints. When an employee complains, the Secretary must investigate, notify the employer, and, on finding reasonable cause to believe the discharge was retaliatory, issue a preliminary order of reinstatement. Roadway discharged Hufstetler for allegedly disabling lights on his assigned truck intentionally. His grievance under the collective bargaining agreement failed. On February 7, 1984, he complained to the Department of Labor that the discharge punished earlier safety complaints. A field investigator interviewed Hufstetler and other employees and took statements supporting him. Roadway met the investigator and submitted a written statement of its reasons, but it was not told the substance of the evidence gathered against it. On January 21, 1985, the Regional Administrator ordered immediate reinstatement with backpay, calling Roadway's explanation conjecture.
sections.Procedural History: Roadway sued in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia seeking an injunction and a declaration that section 405 violated Fifth Amendment due process insofar as it allowed temporary reinstatement without an evidentiary hearing. The court enjoined the reinstatement order and later granted summary judgment for Roadway, 624 F. Supp. 197 (1985). The Secretary appealed directly to the Supreme Court under 28 U.S.C. section 1252. After judgment below, the Secretary held the evidentiary hearing Roadway had requested and issued a final reinstatement order. The Court heard argument on December 3, 1986, and decided the case on April 22, 1987, affirming in part and reversing in part. Justice Marshall announced the judgment and wrote for four Justices.
sections.Issue: Was the appeal moot, given that a final reinstatement order following a full hearing had replaced the preliminary order? On the merits, does the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause require the Secretary, before issuing a preliminary reinstatement order under section 405, to give the employer the substance of the evidence supporting the employee's complaint, and does it require an evidentiary hearing with confrontation and cross-examination of the employee's witnesses before the employer is compelled to put the driver back to work and pay him?
sections.Holding: The appeal was not moot, because the dispute over the adequacy of the Secretary's pre-reinstatement procedures is capable of repetition yet evading review. On the merits the judgment was affirmed in part and reversed in part: the Secretary's procedures denied due process by failing to give Roadway the substance of the evidence supporting Hufstetler's complaint before ordering reinstatement, but due process did not require an evidentiary hearing with confrontation and cross-examination before temporary reinstatement, provided a prompt post-reinstatement hearing is available. Minimum due process for the employer requires notice of the allegations, notice of the substance of the supporting evidence, an opportunity to submit a written response, and an opportunity to meet with the investigator and present statements from rebuttal witnesses.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Marshall applied the Mathews v. Eldridge balance. The employer has a substantial property interest in discharging employees for cause and controlling its workforce, though it is only temporarily deprived of that interest. The Government's interests are strong: highway safety, protection of employees who report violations, and preservation of the employee's livelihood while the case is decided, which the preliminary reinstatement order is designed to serve. The risk of an erroneous deprivation depends on the reliability of the Secretary's fact-finding. Marshall reasoned that an employer given notice of the allegations, the substance of the supporting evidence, a chance to respond in writing and a meeting with the investigator at which it may present rebuttal witnesses receives a reliable initial check against mistaken decisions, comparable to the pretermination process approved in Loudermill and Arnett. Confrontation and cross-examination add reliability but would delay reinstatement and could chill employee complaints, and they are available at the prompt post-reinstatement hearing that the statute contemplates. Because the Secretary's regulations did not require disclosure of the substance of the evidence, and Roadway was not told what its accusers had said, the procedures were constitutionally deficient in that respect. Marshall added that the post-reinstatement hearing must be prompt, noting that the delay in this case had been substantial. Because the Justices divided, the result on each point was determined by counting votes across the separate opinions.

topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The separate opinions disagree over disclosure, confrontation, and timing before preliminary reinstatement while invoking the same general balancing method.

learning.separateOpinions: A fractured Court. Justice Marshall's plurality opinion was joined by Justices Blackmun, Powell and O'Connor. Justice Brennan concurred in part and dissented in part, agreeing that disclosure of the evidence was required but arguing that confrontation and cross-examination were also required before reinstatement where facts were disputed, and objecting to the delay. Justice White, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Scalia, concurred in part and dissented in part, concluding that the procedures Roadway received were adequate and that disclosure of the evidence was not constitutionally required. Justice Stevens dissented in part, concluding that the Government's interest did not justify a reinstatement order based on evidence not disclosed to the employer and tested by cross-examination.
